lessons.title: Policy Rates Explained: Repo, Reverse Repo, SDF, and MSF

body.text: The RBI does not set one interest rate. It builds a corridor: a floor where banks can park spare money, a ceiling where they can borrow in an emergency, and the repo rate in the middle. Overnight rates across India stay inside that corridor, and every loan and deposit rate in the economy is priced off it.

children.text: Chapter 1 explained who decides and what they are aiming for. Chapter 2 opens the toolkit. We start with the most watched tool of all, the policy rates, and follow a single rupee from the RBI's balance sheet to your home loan EMI.
Why Banks Need the RBI Every Single Night

markDefs.definition: The market where banks lend to and borrow from each other overnight, without collateral, to manage day-to-day cash needs.

children.text: Every evening, some banks end the day with more cash than they need, and others fall short. A bank that saw large withdrawals, or disbursed a big corporate loan, needs money overnight. A bank flush with salary credits has money sitting idle. They trade with each other in the
call money market

markDefs.definition: The average interest rate on overnight interbank borrowing in the call money market, weighted by the size of each deal. It is the official operating target of RBI monetary policy.

children.text: The average rate in that market is the
weighted average call rate (WACR)

, and it is the rate the RBI actually tries to steer. The RBI's revised liquidity framework of 2025 kept WACR as the operating target, with the aim of keeping it close to the repo rate. The policy rates are how it does that.

body.title: Name the Target
body.textWithBlank: The overnight interbank rate that the RBI tries to keep close to the repo rate is called the weighted average ___ rate.
body.explanation: The weighted average call rate, or WACR. The repo rate is the signal, but WACR is the operating target: the market rate the RBI actively steers towards the repo rate using its liquidity tools.

body.text: Many personal finance websites still list the reverse repo rate as a key policy rate. It has been stuck at 3.35% since May 2020 and stopped being the floor in April 2022, when the SDF replaced it. If someone tells you the reverse repo rate matters for markets today, they are working from an outdated textbook.

children.text: The Repo Rate: How a Repo Actually Works

markDefs.definition: A short-term loan structured as a sale of securities with a promise to buy them back at a slightly higher price. The price difference is the interest.

children.text: Repo is short for
repurchase agreement
. When a bank borrows from the RBI under repo, it is really selling government securities to the RBI today and agreeing to buy them back tomorrow at a slightly higher price.
Axis Bank, say, is short of ₹2,000 crore on a Tuesday evening.
It hands the RBI government securities worth a little more than ₹2,000 crore, because the RBI applies a small safety margin called a haircut.
The RBI credits ₹2,000 crore to Axis Bank's account.
On Wednesday, Axis Bank pays back ₹2,000 crore plus one day's interest at the repo rate, and gets its securities back.

body.caption: Overnight money market interest in India is calculated on a 365-day year

children.text: In practice, the RBI now lends mostly through variable rate repo auctions, where banks bid for money and the rate can come in slightly above the repo rate. But the repo rate is the anchor all those auctions revolve around, and it is the number the MPC announces.
The Floor: Standing Deposit Facility

When banks have more money than they can lend, they need somewhere safe to put it overnight. The SDF lets them deposit it with the RBI and earn 0.25 percentage points below the repo rate, currently 5.00%.
No bank will lend to another bank below 5.00% overnight, because it can always earn 5.00% risk-free from the RBI. That is what makes the SDF a floor.

body.title: What Does One Night at the SDF Earn?
body.prompt: HDFC Bank has ₹1,000 crore of surplus funds at the end of the day and parks it in the SDF at 5.00% for one night. How much interest does it earn, in rupees? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Interest = ₹1,000 crore × 5.00% × 1/365. ₹1,000 crore is ₹10,000,000,000, so the interest is ₹10,000,000,000 × 0.05 ÷ 365 = ₹13,69,863, about ₹13.7 lakh for one night. Small for a day, but banks move tens of thousands of crores this way.

body.title: Why the RBI Replaced Reverse Repo With the SDF

columns.label: Fixed rate reverse repo (old floor)
points: Banks must receive government securities as collateral
RBI can only absorb as much money as it has securities to give
Became a constraint when surplus liquidity ran into lakhs of crores after COVID
Frozen at 3.35%, now effectively unused as a policy rate

columns.label: Standing Deposit Facility (current floor)
points: No collateral needed, banks simply deposit money
RBI can absorb unlimited surplus, whatever the size
Made possible by an amendment to the RBI Act in 2018
Moves automatically with the repo rate, always 25 bps below it

children.text: The Ceiling: Marginal Standing Facility

markDefs.definition: A deliberately higher interest rate charged to discourage routine use of a facility, so it is used only when there is no cheaper option.

children.text: The MSF is the emergency window. A bank that cannot find money anywhere else can borrow overnight from the RBI at 0.25 percentage points above the repo rate, currently 5.50%. Because it is a
penal rate
, banks use it only when they have to.
Borrowing limit:
banks can pledge government securities, including dipping into their mandatory SLR holdings up to 2% of their net demand and time liabilities.
Timing:
since 1 July 2025, both the SDF and MSF windows open from 7:00 PM to 11:59 PM on all days, including weekends and holidays, after the call money market closes.
Bank Rate:
the RBI's Bank Rate is kept equal to the MSF rate, at 5.50%. It is mainly used to calculate penalties when banks fall short on their CRR and SLR requirements.

body.title: The Cost of Panic Borrowing
body.prompt: A mid-sized bank is forced to borrow ₹500 crore overnight through the MSF at 5.50%, instead of at the 5.25% repo rate. How much extra interest does it pay for that one night, in rupees? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Extra cost = ₹500 crore × (5.50% minus 5.25%) × 1/365 = ₹5,000,000,000 × 0.0025 ÷ 365 = ₹34,247, about ₹34,000. The penalty is not ruinous for one night, but a bank that relies on the MSF night after night is signalling trouble, and the RBI and the market will notice.

children.text: The Corridor in Action

Put the floor and ceiling together and you get a tight band. No bank lends overnight below 5.00%, because the SDF pays that. No bank borrows overnight above 5.50%, because the MSF charges that. So the call rate stays inside the corridor, and the RBI uses liquidity operations to nudge it towards the middle.

body.title: The RBI's Interest Rate Corridor Over Time (%)

series.label: Floor: reverse repo, then SDF from Apr 2022

children.text: Look at 2020. During the COVID shock, the RBI cut the reverse repo far more than the repo rate. By May 2020 the floor was 65 basis points below the repo rate, while the ceiling was only 25 above. That lopsided corridor pushed overnight rates well below the repo rate to flood the system with cheap money. In April 2022, the SDF at 3.75% restored a symmetric 50 basis point corridor as the RBI began to normalise.

body.title: Reading the Corridor
body.question: The repo rate is 5.25%, the SDF rate is 5.00% and the MSF rate is 5.50%. The banking system has a large cash surplus. Where is the call rate most likely to trade?
options: Between 5.00% and 5.25%, closer to the floor
Between 5.25% and 5.50%, closer to the ceiling
body.explanation: With surplus cash, lenders outnumber borrowers, so the call rate drifts down towards the floor. It cannot sustainably fall below 5.00%, because banks would rather earn that from the SDF. This is exactly what happened in August 2026, when WACR traded around 5.18%, below the repo rate, even as the RBI ran reverse repo auctions to soak up excess cash. In a cash shortage, the reverse happens and the call rate drifts up towards 5.50%.

children.text: From the Repo Rate to Your Home Loan EMI

markDefs.definition: A publicly visible interest rate set outside the bank, most commonly the RBI repo rate, to which floating loan rates must be linked. Rates must reset at least once every three months.

children.text: Here is where the corridor reaches your wallet. Since October 2019, banks must link new floating rate retail and MSME loans to an
external benchmark
, and most choose the repo rate. SBI's External Benchmark Linked Rate (EBLR), for example, is the repo rate plus a fixed spread.

body.caption: Effective 15 December 2025, after the December rate cut. Your actual loan rate adds a credit risk premium based on your profile.

children.text: Because the link is mechanical, every repo rate change passes to EBLR borrowers at their next reset, within three months at most. Watch what the 125 basis points of cuts in 2025 did to a typical home loan.

body.caption: P = loan amount, r = monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), n = number of monthly instalments
A ₹50 Lakh, 20-Year Home Loan at EBLR (No Extra Risk Premium)

body.title: How Much Did the 2025 Cuts Save?
body.prompt: Using the table, how much lower is the monthly EMI at 7.90% compared with 9.15%? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹45,470 minus ₹41,511 = ₹3,958 a month. Over a full 20 years at the lower rate, total interest falls by ₹9,50,019. That is what 125 basis points of repo cuts is worth to one family with one home loan. In practice, many banks keep the EMI unchanged and shorten the loan tenure instead, which saves even more interest.

children.text: Use the calculator above with your own loan. Try your current rate, then subtract 0.25%, and see what one MPC decision does to your EMI.

body.text: Older loans linked to MCLR or base rate adjust much more slowly, because those benchmarks depend on the bank's own funding costs, not directly on the repo rate. If your loan predates October 2019 and you never switched, you may not have received the full benefit of the 2025 cuts. Ask your bank about switching to the external benchmark.

body.title: Go Deeper: Variable Rate Auctions, the Real Workhorse

children.text: The fixed-rate windows set the corridor, but most day-to-day liquidity management happens through auctions. When the system is short of cash, the RBI conducts variable rate repo (VRR) auctions to lend. When there is surplus, it conducts variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb it.

Under the revised framework issued in September 2025, the RBI discontinued the 14-day auctions as its main operation. Short-term liquidity is now managed mainly through 7-day VRR and VRRR auctions, supported by operations of other tenors from overnight up to 14 days at the RBI's discretion. Longer-lasting liquidity is managed through open market operations and forex swaps, which you will study in Lesson 3 of this chapter.

body.title: Explain the Headline
body.scenario: A business channel ticker reads: "Call rates spike to 5.48% as advance tax outflows drain bank liquidity; RBI holds repo at 5.25%." Your colleague asks: "If the RBI didn't change rates, how did borrowing costs go up?"
body.prompt: Explain what happened using the corridor, and say what the RBI is likely to do next.
body.modelAnswer: The repo rate is the policy signal, but the actual overnight rate is set by supply and demand for cash. Around advance tax dates, companies pull large sums from bank accounts to pay tax to the government, and that money temporarily leaves the banking system. Banks suddenly have less cash to lend, so the call rate rises towards the 5.50% MSF ceiling. It cannot rise much above 5.50%, because any bank can borrow from the MSF at that rate. The RBI is likely to respond by injecting liquidity through variable rate repo auctions, which pulls the call rate back towards 5.25%. Nothing about monetary policy has changed; this is day-to-day liquidity management inside the corridor.

cards.definition: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks against government securities. The main policy signal set by the MPC. Currently 5.25%.
Where banks park surplus money with the RBI without collateral. The floor of the corridor, at repo minus 25 bps.
The emergency overnight borrowing window at repo plus 25 bps. The ceiling of the corridor.
The old floor, frozen at 3.35% since May 2020 and replaced by the SDF in April 2022.
Weighted average call rate: the overnight interbank rate, and the RBI's operating target.
The band between the SDF floor and MSF ceiling within which overnight rates trade.
External Benchmark Linked Rate: a loan rate linked directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, reset at least every three months.

body.description: The RBI homepage shows the current policy repo, SDF, MSF, Bank Rate, CRR and SLR in one panel. Check it after every MPC meeting.

body.title: Apply It to Your Own Money
steps: Find your home, car or personal loan sanction letter and check which benchmark it is linked to: EBLR, RLLR, MCLR or base rate
Note your bank's current EBLR and work out your spread above the repo rate
Check when your loan rate last reset, and whether the December 2025 cut has passed through
Use the EMI calculator to see what a further 25 bps cut or hike would do to your EMI
Visit the RBI homepage and confirm today's repo, SDF and MSF rates

points: The RBI runs a corridor: SDF as the floor at 5.00%, the repo rate in the middle at 5.25%, and MSF as the ceiling at 5.50%.
The repo rate is the policy signal, but the RBI's operating target is the weighted average call rate, which it tries to keep close to the repo rate.
The SDF replaced the fixed rate reverse repo as the floor in April 2022 because it needs no collateral. The reverse repo rate of 3.35% is no longer a meaningful policy rate.
The MSF is a penal emergency window; the Bank Rate equals the MSF rate and is used for CRR and SLR shortfall penalties.
Surplus liquidity pushes the call rate towards the floor, and tight liquidity pushes it towards the ceiling, even when the repo rate is unchanged.
EBLR loans pass repo changes to borrowers within three months. On a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan, the 125 bps of 2025 cuts lowered the EMI by about ₹4,000 a month.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment or borrowing advice. Rates are as of the RBI's August 2026 policy and SBI's EBLR effective 15 December 2025; your loan rate depends on your lender and credit profile.
